x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
"LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure"

What happens if you train an LLM that has only ever seen elementary school knowledge?

This paper trains a 5B model from scratch on 88B tokens filtered to K-5 content, creating an explicit boundary around what the model was exposed to during pretraining.

Scaling, few-shot prompting, and even SFT + GRPO improve capabilities within that boundary, but do little for genuinely out-of-scope reasoning.

This gave insights on how pretraining exposure may set a much harder capability ceiling than we think, with post-training mostly amplifying what the model already learned rather than creating entirely new capabilities.

https://t.co/8UTF6CM8vG

For a limited time, you can revise your paper's alphaXiv blog

Your revisions will be published as "author-verified" and shared with our community

We're collaborating with researchers from Ai2, Ohio State & U of Utah to learn how AI-generated research blogs can better serve authors and readers

Sign up here: https://t.co/hm1HuBtSSY

"Maglev: Sliding Recurrent Memory"

Transformers can either keep the full history with expensive attention, or use a sliding window that is efficient but forgets anything that falls outside it.

This paper makes that forgotten history recurrent. So they used a stronger prefiller that creates memory targets in parallel, and a sliding-window Transformer that learns to reproduce and carry those memories forward through its KV cache.

The prefiller is then removed at inference, so the model gets persistent nonlinear memory with fixed-size attention and KV cache, while still being trained with parallel Transformer passes.

https://t.co/2N4QrBagxt

tweets.text:
3. AI has landed on top of existing work rather than replacing it 😭

Teams now spent more time chatting with AI and delegating to agents but didn't spend any less time on existing work.

I think this is because expectations for what any function can accomplish are simply much higher now.

2. Non-engineers are shipping more code

PMs attaching pull requests rose from 3% to 10% in two years. Designers went from 1% to 8%, and founders are second only to engineers at 23%.

I'm actually surprised that designers are slightly behind PMs on this, given the rise of design engineer roles.

Over 40K product teams use @Linear so their report on AI usage is pretty interesting.

Some observations:

1. PM AI adoption is rising the fastest

All functions increased their AI adoption, but product grew the fastest, from 12% to 34%.

When I was a PM, I had a lot of busywork like monitoring Slack, updating docs, summarizing feedback, and more - all stuff that agents are great at.
